newsitem.title: UK: Fall in UK retail sales unlikely to last - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Fall in UK retail sales unlikely to last - analysts.

text.p: A fall in British retail sales in September was little more than a blip and does not reawaken the interest rate debate or suggest consumers are withdrawing into their shells, analysts said on Wednesday.

Sales dropped 0.3 percent in September, more sharply than market forecasts, but the decline was concentrated in clothing and footwear sales. And anecdotal evidence for early October suggests spending has stormed ahead again.
"The decline was sharper than the market was looking for but it's just a blip," said Ciaran Barr at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Economists had forecast sales would fall just 0.1 percent in September. "But the three-month trend shows things have really picked up," Barr said.
Sales for the three months to September were 3.4 percent higher than the same period a year ago, the highest rate since December 1994, the Office for National Statistics said.

Surveys from the British Retail Consortium and Confederation of British Industry had suggested a small drop in sales. So any market relief will be short-lived, particularly since John Lewis Partnership's sales figures and weekly M0 money supply data, suggest a healthy boost for retail sales in October.

"There is little doubt that high street spending remains on a firm upward trend. Early figures from John Lewis already point to a rebound in October," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

Unlisted stores and supermarkets group John Lewis Partnership Plc's weekly store sales rose about 14 percent year-on-year on average in September. For the first three weeks of October, they have increased by as much as 20 percent.
Looking at the breakdown of the September data, a three percent monthly fall in textile, clothing and footwear sales dragged the overall retail sales index down.
Within that, footwear sales dropped by 12 percent in value terms in September. That exerted the major downward effect, the ONS said.

Barr noted the 0.3 percent fall in overall sales volumes followed a 0.9 percent leap in August. "And the same applies to clothing and footwear sales. Most of this month's decline came from there, following a hefty rise in August."
Textile, clothing and footwear sales jumped 2.2 percent in August.
The markets could take some comfort though, since clothing and footwear prices leapt by 5.2 percent in September.
"Consumers are not yet willing to abandon the bargain- hunting mentality and still baulk at paying higher non-sale prices," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
He said that sort of evidence would allow Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to ward off Bank of England Governor Eddie George's campaign to raise interest rates.
Barr said the pound, up more than six percent since early August on a trade-weighted basis, carried on rising it could delay an increase in 5.75 percent base rates.
But he forecast a half-point hike in the first quarter of 1997, probably before elections which are due by May next year.
"The consumer side will only grow from here," Barr said.

But he conceded that although high street spending was solid, it was falling short of the boom conditions of the late 1980s. "There's a firm underlying trend there but we're not back to the forthiness we saw in the late '80s."
Loynes at HSBC agreed.
"For the time being at least these numbers will help to allay fears of a return to a 1980s-style consumer boom."
He said the focus would now switch to Friday's third quarter GDP data which are forecast to show healthy 0.7 percent quarter-on-quarter growth.
